entries.title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
entries.content:
Enterprise Article

Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.

These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research.

Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

Helping researchers check the work

For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

Keep scientific judgment in the loop

Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”

Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.

Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said.

Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research.

These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work.

The same tension applies to safeguards built into AI systems. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. Meanwhile, participants working with sensitive human-subject data wanted stronger guarantees about privacy, access, and how information would be used.

Both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry.

This is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work.

Build AI agents alongside scientists

Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology.

Researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities.

It will also require continued collaboration. Our study is exploratory; the findings come from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. Participants discussed both the generative AI tools they use today and what they anticipate from more autonomous systems. Their perspectives identify important concerns and design priorities, rather than establishing a consensus about how AI should be used in science.

Still, they offer a path forward. At Ai2, we believe AI can accelerate scientific discovery while preserving the openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny that make research trustworthy. Through our broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents, we aim to put those principles into practice. That means working with scientists to identify worthwhile uses for agents and translating their concerns into concrete evaluations, in addition to making it easier to understand both what these systems accomplish and how they accomplish it.

The promise of scientific AI isn't simply that researchers can pass off more work. It's that they can pursue questions that might otherwise be out of reach while retaining the knowledge, judgment, and agency needed to make discoveries that are their own.

entries.title: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA
entries.content:
Enterprise Article

Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps.

The use case: a Farm Assistant

A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:

  1. Listens and turns the speech into text.
  2. Searches a 154-page agricultural handbook, which is written in English.
  3. Answers in two to four spoken sentences, in the language the question was asked in, using only what the handbook says.
  4. Speaks the answer back and shows the source pages, so the answer can be checked.

If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

Where CUGA fits

CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:

  • One agent, any model. Switch between watsonx and OpenAI with one setting.
  • The knowledge engine. Parse a PDF, chunk it, embed it, and search it locally with 
    agent.knowledge.search()
    .
  • Conversation threads. Each question gets a fresh thread, so one person's language or context never leaks into another's.

The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

audio ──▶ speech-to-text ──▶ knowledge.search ──▶ CUGA (grounded answer) ──▶ text-to-speech ──▶ audio

Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

The hard part is not the voice

Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use 

intfloat/multilingual-e5-large
), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

Making it sound right and keeping it safe

A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:

  • Write for the ear. Markdown, bullet points, citation tags and bracketed translations such as "millet (बाजरा)" all sound wrong when read aloud. The prompt asks the model not to produce them, and a light formatter strips any that slip through before speech.
  • Keep guardrails cheap. Simple input checks catch obvious off-topic questions. If one gets through, the model starts its reply with 
    OFF_TOPIC
    , and the app swaps in a polite redirect. No second LLM call, so the voice path stays fast.
  • Ground every answer. The model sees only the retrieved passages, is told not to use outside knowledge, and the page sources are shown to the user.
  • Keep keys out of the server. With the Sarvam option, the browser talks to Sarvam directly. The server receives only text and never sees the user's key.

Try it

You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:

Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

Beyond farming: Scaling for Bharat

Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core.

Learn more about CUGA

New to CUGA? Here are some places to start:

  • cuga.dev: the CUGA home page.
  • CUGA on GitHub: the open-source harness (Apache 2.0). Star it, file issues, or pick up a good first issue.
  • CUGA documentation: setup, the SDK, knowledge, policies and configuration.
  • CUGA Apps gallery on GitHub: the source for the apps in the Hugging Face Space.

Spaces you can try in your browser:

  • CUGA Agent: the general-purpose agent, running on a demo CRM scenario.
  • CUGA Apps: launch working CUGA apps from one dashboard.
  • CUGA Policy Playground: two live agents side by side, one with policies and one without.

More CUGA posts on the Hugging Face blog:

  • CUGA on Hugging Face: Democratizing Configurable AI Agents: the introduction to CUGA and its configurable reasoning modes.
  • Build real agentic apps using CUGA: two dozen working examples on a lightweight harness: the app gallery this voice agent belongs to.
  • Same Model, Different Harness: CUGA, Hermes, and Deep Agents — When to Pick CUGA?: how much the harness matters when the model stays the same.

entries.title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
entries.content:
Update on GitHub

Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here.

One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs (

sm100
), leaving out 
sm120
cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ.

We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an 

nvidia-rtx-pro-6000
Inference Endpoint. Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the 
inference-optimisation
 skill, the 
hf
CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs, and let it run experiments for an afternoon.

Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in 

NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb
.

The setup

The 

inference-optimisation
skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script (
bench.py
):
  1. Measure the hardware and estimate theoretical ceilings before tuning.
  2. Change one variable at a time and bracket every candidate between two control runs (
    control → candidate → control
    ). Keep a change only if it beats both controls without regressing other metrics.
  3. Log every run in 
    PLAN.md
    , including regressions and dead ends.
  4. Pass long-context, concurrency, and greedy-equivalence checks before declaring a winner.

bench.py
measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled.

The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure:

  • HF Jobs for compute. The 
    rtx-pro-6000
    Job flavor uses the same GPU as the 
    nvidia-rtx-pro-6000
    Inference Endpoint ($2.75/h for both), so Job numbers transfer directly. A ~150-line driver (
    jobs/driver.py
    ) takes a list of server configs, starts each one, runs an unmeasured warmup, calls 
    bench.py
    unmodified, shuts the server down, and prints one ledger line per run. Because Jobs run on separate machines, the agent swept SGLang (
    lmsysorg/sglang:inkling-2-mini
    ) and vLLM nightly (
    vllm/vllm-openai:nightly
    ) in parallel.
  • CPU Jobs for reading engine source. When a flag was undocumented, the agent ran a cheap 
    cpu-upgrade
    Job to grep the installed Python package inside the container. That is how it found SGLang's 
    SGLANG_OPT_*
    environment variables and vLLM's 
    speculative-config
    fields.
  • Inference Endpoints for deployment, created via 
    hf endpoints deploy
    using the exact image digest and flags that passed verification.

The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with 

--attention-backend fa4
and no speculative decoding.

Results

Single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate.

Config (1× RTX PRO 6000)1-user decode (tok/s)8-user aggregate (tok/s)Prefill 4K / 32K (tok/s)TTFT
SGLang, no speculation (baseline)134–139543–59818.7–19.1K / 16.9–19.1K41–114 ms
vLLM, no speculation157.063820.7K / 20.7K33 ms
SGLang + DSpark (8 drafts)166.6— ¹18.0–19.5K / 18.9–19.1K38–51 ms
vLLM + DSpark (7 drafts)190.671620.7K / 20.6K40 ms
Deployed endpoint (over the internet)194.967311.7K / 19.2K ²198 ms ²

¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps 

--max-running-requests
at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM. ² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip.

All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB:

vllm serve thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini \
  --tool-call-parser inkling \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --reasoning-parser inkling \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'

Both 

num_speculative_tokens: 7
and 
draft_sample_method: "probabilistic"
were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to 
greedy
draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work).

Why it stops around 190 tok/s

Before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job (1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s. Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits.

Speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s. At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth, so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer.

What didn't work

Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower:

vLLM

LeverResult
Shorter draft length (3–6)Rejected at startup; requires 
num_speculative_tokens = 7
(checkpoint block size − 1).		 
draft_sample_method: "greedy"
 −11% at temperature 1.0 (168.6 vs ~190.4 tok/s).
rejection_sample_method: "block"
 190.1 vs 190.3–190.5 for controls; no effect.
enable_adaptive_verification
 Assertion error at startup for the Inkling 2 drafter.
draft_lm_head_quantization: "fp8"
 Only supported for DeepSeek DSpark drafters.

We also skipped 

rejection_sample_method: "fly"
and 
"synthetic"
on purpose because they alter the output distribution, and we wanted a strictly lossless speedup.

SGLang

LeverResult
Shorter draft length (3–6)Rejected at startup; requires 
--speculative-num-draft-tokens 8
(
gamma + 1
for the bundled drafter).		 
SGLANG_ENABLE_NV_MEGA_RUNTIME_OPTIMIZATION=1
 +4% once, failed to reproduce against fresh controls.
SGLANG_OPT_USE_FUSED_DRAFT_SAMPLE=1
 +2%, within run-to-run noise.
SGLANG_OPT_MOE_QUANT_ONCE=1
 +1%, within run-to-run noise.
SGLANG_DSPARK_USE_GREEDY_DRAFT=1
 −9% at temperature 1.0 (156.8 vs ~172 tok/s).

Benchmarking gotchas

A few measurement issues caught us along the way:

  • Triton JIT during timed prefill. vLLM's first 4K prefill came back at 202 tok/s instead of 20K because Triton was compiling kernels during the timed request. Running an unmeasured warmup across prompt lengths and concurrency fixed 4K prefill, though the first run in each Job still under-reported 32K prefill due to last-chunk shape differences (flagged in the ledger).
  • Orphaned servers holding GPU memory. The initial driver stopped servers via a PID saved from 
    setsid … &
    , which is not guaranteed to match the process group ID. The previous server stayed alive on port 8000, broke the next launch, and turned into a zombie that still passed 
    kill -0
    . Managing the process with 
    subprocess.Popen(start_new_session=True)
    and waiting until both GPU memory and port 8000 are free fixed it.
  • Hidden OOM errors in vLLM logs. vLLM + DSpark twice died with 
    "Engine core initialization failed"
    at the end of the log while the real causes sat 200 lines up. First, the default 1M-token KV cache needed 52.6 GiB with only 48.1 GiB free alongside the drafter (
    --max-model-len 262144
    fixed this). Next, because vLLM v0.34.0 raised the default 
    --gpu-memory-utilization
    from 
    0.92
    to 
    1.0
    , the KV cache claimed the remaining VRAM and OOMed the drafter's 5 GiB allocation (
    --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85
    fixed this). The driver now prints every error line from the server log instead of just the tail.
  • Engine variance. Across identical runs with speculation, vLLM stayed within 0.4% while SGLang swung by ±4.5%. That was wide enough to make 
    SGLANG_ENABLE_NV_MEGA_RUNTIME_OPTIMIZATION=1
    look like a +4% win on its first run before repeat controls ruled it out.

Verification and deployment

Before deploying, we pinned the exact vLLM nightly digest (

vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6…
, build 
0.34.0rc1.dev1235+gf2f9edcac
) and ran the acceptance gates inside a Job:
GateResult
Needle retrieval at ~50% context (126,537 tokens)3/3, TTFT 12.5 s
Needle retrieval at ~95% context (249,970 tokens)3/3, TTFT 28.7 s
Concurrent soak (4 × ~58K-token requests)4/4 succeeded, 3/3 retrieval each
Greedy equivalence, DSpark vs no speculation (6 prompts, temp 0)6/6 byte-identical
Single-user decode on pinned image189.9 / 190.2 tok/s

Once those passed, we deployed the endpoint with a single 

hf endpoints deploy
command, pinning both the image digest and model revision (authenticated access, scale-to-zero after 60 idle minutes):
hf endpoints deploy inkling2mini-tuned-dspark --namespace  \
  --repo thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini --revision 7a67ae2314b44ef05c87fd1d4d311c58aaeb18f6 \
  --framework custom --custom-image "vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6ee3aac77f3158e80ed79ec425db3a53f7cd666bf1954e96abfaf19a7" \
  --health-route /health --port 8000 \
  --vendor aws --region us-east-2 --accelerator gpu --instance-type nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 --instance-size x1 \
  --min-replica 0 --max-replica 1 --scale-to-zero-timeout 60 --type authenticated \
  --container-command "vllm serve" \
  --container-args "/repository --served-model-name thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --tool-call-parser inkling --enable-auto-tool-choice --reasoning-parser inkling --max-model-len 262144 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --speculative-config '{\"method\":\"dspark\",\"num_speculative_tokens\":7,\"draft_sample_method\":\"probabilistic\"}'"

Running 

bench.py
against the live endpoint gave 194.9 tok/s single-user, matching the Job runs once network latency is accounted for.

Everything from this run (

PLAN.md
, 
THEORY.md
, 
jobs/driver.py
, 
submit.sh
, 
deploy.sh
, and the raw 
ledger-*.jsonl
files) is in 
NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb
. To reuse the loop on another model, put your candidate and control server commands into a 
configs/plan-*.json
file and submit it to whichever HF Jobs GPU flavor matches your target endpoint.

entries.title: Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton
entries.content:
Enterprise + Article

TL;DR

Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. This tutorial covers simulation training, evaluation, export, and real-robot deployment.

Introduction

A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy.

NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing.

1. Set Microduck obstacle avoidance in Isaac Lab

For simulation and training, prepare:

  • A Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. See the Isaac Lab installation guide for platform requirements.

  • Git with Git LFS, and the uv package manager.

For physical-robot testing, prepare:

  • A configured Microduck. Load the same backlash walking-policy export used by the navigation task.

  • A supported ToF sensor with its configuration recorded.

  • A paired gamepad and a level test area with obstacles.

Quick install

Install uv if it is not already installed. Then clone the exp/microduck branch of the Isaac Lab repository and install its dependencies:

git lfs install
git clone --branch exp/microduck https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git
cd IsaacLab
uv sync --frozen

Once setup is complete, list the available Microduck environments and presets:

uv run isaaclab list_envs --keyword MicroDuck --show_presets

Download the walking policy

Download and export the upstream backlash walking checkpoint once before training. The obstacle avoidance task loads the exported walking policy automatically.

uv run isaaclab play \
  --task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \
  --rl_library rsl_rl --checkpoint pretrained \
  --num_envs 1 --visualizer none \
  --video newton_gl --video_length 1 \
  presets=backlash

2. Build the obstacle course

The environment combines simple primitives with OpenUSD assets available through SimReady Central on Hugging Face. We use a cardboard box, office bin, bedside cabinet alongside cones. From the IsaacLab repository root, download the pinned box, bin and cabinet packages into assets/simready.

uvx --from huggingface-hub hf download nvidia/simready-assets \
  --repo-type dataset \
  --revision 9d4556bfe80868c1d27a7a7ba1c2774e63e8cedd \
  --include "box_cardboard_a01/*" \
  --include "trashCan_office_black_a03/*" \
  --include "table_bedside_b01/*" \
  --local-dir ./assets/simready

At each episode reset, the environment code automatically samples a layout, shuffles the props, and varies their placement and rotation. Most courses scatter obstacles ahead of the duck, with a smaller mix of clear paths, barriers and passages. The code also mirrors layouts and mixes aligned and staggered rows.

Goals start ahead of the duck. Movement commands guide it toward the goal while the policy adjusts them around obstacles.

Figure 1. Varied obstacle-course layouts with SimReady assets and primitive geometry.

3. Understand how ToF sensing guides the walking policy

The 

IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck
task separates obstacle avoidance from balance. A navigation policy uses ToF sensing to adjust forward, lateral, and yaw commands at 50 Hz. The frozen walking policy then converts those commands into joint actions, allowing the robot to learn obstacle avoidance without retraining its walking behavior.

During training, the navigation policy’s actor receives ToF history and body and controller state available on the real robot. Its critic has access to additional simulation state to guide learning, but is not needed for deployment.

Rewards encourage progress toward the goal, safe arrivals, and movement around obstacles. Following a movement command earns credit only when the robot makes progress with sufficient clearance; risky approaches reduce that credit. Penalties discourage fast approaches, abrupt command changes, collisions, and falls.

The obstacle-avoidance task lives in 

isaaclab_tasks.contrib.microduck_obstacle
. Its configuration is in 
obstacle_avoidance_env_cfg.py
, ToF sensing is in 
sensors.py
, and actions, commands, observations and rewards are organized under 
mdp/
.

Model the ToF sensor

MicroDuckToFCamera extends Newton’s LegacyMultiMeshRayCasterCamera to model the VL53L5CX—a compact time-of-flight (ToF) sensor on the microduck that measures distance across an 8×8 grid at 15Hz. The simulated sensor has a 45° field of view and a 0.12–4 m range. It follows the duck’s head, with placement similar to the sensor on the real duck.

Real recordings informed the sensor placement and floor readings in simulation. Training adds noise, delays and missing measurements—including near the grid’s edges—to expose the policy to imperfect data. The excerpt below shows selected sensor settings already included in the task configuration. You do not need to edit or run this code separately.

# Selected settings; mount and raycast targets omitted.
head_tof = MicroDuckToFCameraCfg(
    prim_path=MICRODUCK_HEAD_BODY_PATH,
    update_period=1.0 / 15.0,
    pattern_cfg=patterns.PinholeCameraPatternCfg(
        focal_length=1.0, width=8, height=8,
        horizontal_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE,
        vertical_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE,
    ),
    randomization=ToFRandomizationCfg(
        mount_pitch_degrees=(-10.0, 10.0),
        mount_height_m=(-0.02, 0.02),
        floor_validity_midpoint_offset_m=(0.0, 0.13),
        near_floor_edge_impairment_probability=0.5,
    ),
    data_types=["distance_to_image_plane", "distance_to_camera"],
    max_distance=TOF_MAX_RANGE,
    depth_clipping_behavior="zero",
)

4. Train the Microduck policy across parallel environments

Train the navigation policy with PPO across 16,384 parallel environments for 1,500 training iterations. Its actor, critic, normalizers, and optimizer start fresh. The task configuration loads the fixed walking checkpoint, robot model, and obstacle assets.

The 16,384 environments shown here are configurable, not a minimum requirement. Lower 

--num_envs
to fit your GPU’s available memory. With fewer environments collecting experience in parallel, reaching comparable policy performance may require more training iterations and longer training time. We also trained this policy on NVIDIA DGX Spark in approximately 6 hours using 4,096 parallel environments for 3,000 PPO updates, demonstrating a smaller-scale configuration for the same workflow.

Run this command to train the policy:

uv run isaaclab train \
  --task IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck \
  --rl_library rsl_rl \
  --num_envs 16384 \
  --max_iterations 1500 \
  --seed 42 \
  --device cuda:0 \
  --visualizer none \
  presets=backlash

Figure 2. Parallel MicroDuck obstacle-avoidance simulation

5. Inspect behavior and export the policy to ONNX

Playback uses the same props, primitives, frozen walker and sensor randomization as training, with a different seed for new obstacle arrangements.

Navigation checkpoints are saved under 

logs/rsl_rl/microduck_obstacle_avoidance_tof_flat_backlash//
relative to the repository root. Choose a 
model_.pt
file from your run and replace 
/absolute/path/to/model.pt
below with its path. This plays the policy, opens the Newton viewer and records 20 seconds of simulation. Set --viz to none for headless recording.
uv run --extra video isaaclab play \
  --task IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck \
  --rl_library rsl_rl \
  --checkpoint /absolute/path/to/model.pt \
  --num_envs 1 \
  --seed 6173 \
  --device cuda:0 \
  --viz newton_gl \
  --video newton_gl \
  --video_length 1000 \
  presets=backlash

Playback saves TorchScript and ONNX models in the checkpoint’s exported folder. Keep the ONNX data file alongside the model.

Figure 3. Cone-course evaluation with requested motion, policy steering, and ToF input overlays.

6. Test obstacle avoidance on a real Microduck

These deployment tools run the navigation model on a laptop and send adjusted gamepad commands to the walking policy on the robot. Use the same walking policy that was used during navigation training.

Section 1 saves the walker’s ONNX export to 

.pretrained_checkpoints/rsl_rl/https/omniverse-content-production.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/Assets/Isaac/6.2/Isaac/IsaacLab/PretrainedCheckpoints/rsl_rl/exported/policy.onnx
, relative to the Isaac Lab repository root.

Load that walking policy using Pollen’s policy-loading guide. The deployment README includes the transfer steps, including how to package an ONNX export that uses an external data file.

From your Isaac Lab checkout, set up SSH access and check inference with the robot standing upright and still:

cd scripts/deploy/microduck_tof_nav
ssh-copy-id microduck@ROBOT_HOST
uv run nav_pad.py --robot ROBOT_HOST \
  --model /absolute/path/to/navigation/exported/policy.onnx \
  --dry-run --seconds 30

Dry-run copies the helpers and streams sensor data, but sends no movement commands. Watch the proposed commands as obstacles enter the sensor’s view. Keep the navigation ONNX and any companion .data file together.

Once those checks pass, start supervised gamepad navigation:

uv run nav_pad.py --robot ROBOT_HOST \
  --model /absolute/path/to/navigation/exported/policy.onnx

Hold the stick forward to request movement; the policy adjusts the command to avoid obstacles. Release the stick to stop, press X to toggle navigation, and use Ctrl-C to end the session. Forward speed is capped at 0.15 m/s by default, with an additional close-obstacle brake and stale-input stopping. Start in a clear area and verify stopping before testing a course.

See the deployment README for controls, logs and troubleshooting.

Figure 4. Microduck steers around cones using its 8×8 ToF sensor, with real footage on the left and a 3D rebuild from its logs on the right. Blue shows the policy steering, purple shows the operator intervention.

7. Explore other locomotion skills for Microduck in Isaac Lab

The Microduck task collection includes velocity tracking on flat and rough terrain; stand-up recovery, sit–stand transitions, and walking with fall recovery (VelStand); ball kicking, ground picking, and forward rolls (Roulade). Roller-skating tasks add velocity tracking and swizzle motion, crouch-gliding, slope descent, standing up on skates, and spins.

Figure 5. Fifteen Microduck task views: flat and rough-terrain walking, recovery, object interaction, and roller-skating motions.

Build your next policy

Start with the first Microduck tutorial, then choose a task from the Microduck task collection to build your next policy in Isaac Lab with Newton. Explore new behaviors by changing commands, rewards, or environments—from rough-terrain walking to perception-driven obstacle avoidance. Evaluate your policy on scenes outside the training set before testing on the robot.

Resources

  • Microduck home page (ordering, quick start, installation)

  • Train a Microduck in Isaac Lab

  • Train Robots to Navigate with AI agents, NVIDIA Isaac Lab and RTX Spark

  • Train in Simulation, Deploy on a Real Robot: Microduck with Isaac Lab 3.0

  • Isaac Lab installation guide

  • Microduck training environments and configuration

  • Newton-based BAM actuator documentation

  • Microduck Arena and ONNX submission guide

  • Explore SimReady Central for more simulation-ready OpenUSD assets from OEMs and asset providers.

  • Learn how to Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

  • Microduck robot software and deployment guide

Acknowledgments

This workflow builds on Pollen Robotics’ Microduck hardware and software, the original Microduck reinforcement-learning project, BAM actuator modeling work, and the Isaac Lab and Newton integrations.

entries.title: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
entries.content:
Update on GitHub

Overview

AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on.

Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it.

The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments.

This guide covers four things:

  • Three eras of evaluation (section 1). Evaluations moved from checking answers, to checking what an agent did, to checking what a team of agents produces. Each step adds software that can change the score.
  • The steps in an agentic evaluation (section 2). We follow one task through eight steps, from the claim to the reported score. The full walkthrough, with commands, is in Appendix A.
  • When a benchmark is wrong (section 3). Errors in tasks and graders are common. We look at how they are found and corrected.
  • What to open strategically and why (section 4). A table sets out, component by component, what to share and what can stay protected.

In the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent. The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across.

1. Introduction: how evaluation design has changed

AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes.

Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms, teams managed by an orchestrator, and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work. Figure 1 shows a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations.

Figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced.

We’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench, researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed.

The anatomy of an agentic evaluation

Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation.

There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately.

Why benchmark release decisions matter

Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party, and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough.

At the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis says 60% of its Intelligence Index v5, announced in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations, where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable.

2. Building an eval: what to reuse, adapt, and validate

With the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation.

We work through eight steps: define the claim, find a task, run it unchanged, adapt it, check the evaluation, read the traces, report the score, and compare models. We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A. Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example.

Figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel shows what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results.

Method

Claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A). For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio (the intensity of one peak relative to another, which can indicate defects in the material; we also call it the defect ratio), and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Starting task and baseline. We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. Harbor is an open source evaluation harness, and Terminal-Bench is an open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a terminal. We first ran the task's reference solution, which passed, and then ran the original task three times with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI. Harbor ran inside an HF Job, each rollout used its own HF Sandbox, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. Only the agent harness needed no new work. Every other component needed checking or new work, which we list part by part at the end of Appendix A.

Adaptation. We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. The new instructions state the units and parameter definitions that the original left implicit. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

Checks. Before executing more model runs, we tested the evaluation itself. We ran the reference solution, an agent that does nothing, and a shortcut that skips the required work. The reference solution should pass every task, and the other two should fail. Our shortcut read the height of each peak straight from the data and guessed the widths. It returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself.

Shortcut. We also tested a shortcut to check how robust the evaluation is against cheating. Our shortcut is a short script that skips the actual fitting. It reads the tallest point of each peak straight from the data, guesses the peak widths, and divides the D height by the G height. Even so, it returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks, so a grader that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks. We added checks on each fitted peak, and the final verifier rejects it.

Results

Figure 4. What we learned by measuring different aspects while building the evaluation. (A) Testing the grader with a shortcut showed that a ratio-only check could be fooled. (B) Reading gpt-oss-120b’s traces showed that most of its failures came from stopping early. (C) Running other models showed that the tasks can be solved. Appendix A has the detailed results in Figure 7 (how gpt-oss-120b’s attempts ended), Figure 8 (all six models) and Figure 9 (when each model said it was done).

Baseline. On the original task, gpt-oss-120b passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

Traces and score. On the eight adapted tasks, we ran three rollouts per task. The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called 

mark_task_complete
in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file. Several of these began with a script failing because NumPy or SciPy was missing, which the task expects the agent to install. Most failures therefore came from stopping early or from a missing package, and only two of the 13 failed the fit check (Figure 7 in Appendix A). Our pass@3 was 7/8: seven tasks succeeded at least once. Our pass^3 was 1/8: one task succeeded every time. Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more. The mean pass rate was 0.46, with a standard error of about 0.11 when rollouts are clustered by task. A repeat run passed 10 of 24. With eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.

Model comparison. We then compared six models on the same eight tasks (Figure 4). Several providers can serve the same open-weight model with different quantization and context limits, so we pinned one provider per model. With DeepInfra pinned as the provider, gpt-oss-120b passed 13 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the earlier run, which used the default provider. Only gpt-oss-120b declared completion in its first response, in 22 of 24 rollouts. None of the other five models did so in any rollout (Figure 9 in Appendix A). The comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

3. Bitter lessons: when a benchmark is wrong

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio without fitting a spectrum. A verifier that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks on all eight tasks. We found it by trying to break the grader with a solution we knew was incomplete, then added checks on the fitted spectrum (Appendix A, Step 5).

The shortcut got the right answer for the wrong reason, like a student who copies the final number without the working. The lesson for us was to test what the output demonstrates. A faster valid method should pass; a method that skips a required skill should not. Domain experts can help set tolerances so the verifier accepts alternative correct fits without accepting work that misses the point of the task.

Such errors are common, and they move scores considerably. A review of agentic benchmarks found that flaws in task setup or reward design can shift measured performance by up to 100% in relative terms.

Public review is essential for correcting benchmarks

Public review can expose errors in instructions and tests that benchmark builders missed. Terminal-Bench 2.1 fixed 28 of its 89 tasks after user reports, including one whose tests expected Spark SQL while its instructions asked for PostgreSQL, and agent rankings stayed stable through the correction.

Access to the evidence also determines how much work an outside audit takes. CritPt keeps its reference solutions private, so the physicists who audited it had to solve the problems themselves before finding errors in 21 of the 56 challenges they reviewed. The authors then released a corrected version. OpenAI's audit of SWE-bench Verified found material issues in 59.4% of the 138 problems it examined, working from tasks and tests that anyone can read. For a builder, outside scrutiny is part of validation: publish what reviewers need to challenge a task, give them a way to report problems, and record what changed.

Similar flaws emerged in SWE-bench Pro. In July 2026 OpenAI estimated that about 30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks were broken and withdrew its recommendation to adopt it. Benchmark validation needs to continue after release.

Check the claim as well as the code

A consistent score can still measure the wrong thing. Measuring what Matters, a review of 445 LLM benchmarks by 29 expert reviewers, found recurring patterns in tasks and metrics that undermine construct validity: whether the tasks and metrics support claims about the intended capability.

For example, fitting synthetic spectra does not establish that an agent can review lab reports. That may also require recognizing a poor measurement or asking for help. If every task supplies a usable spectrum, the test cannot show whether the agent knows when a fit would be inappropriate.

Harder Than the Task extends this concern to organizational work, where authority, distributed knowledge, and dependencies can decide success. Its authors find that fewer than one quarter of prominent benchmarks claim to cover any such dimension. An agent may need calibration data from another team or permission to replace a measurement, and supplying everything at the outset removes those difficulties. If they matter to the claim, they belong in the evaluation. If they do not, it is enough to say that they remain untested.

Each error is worth a short record: the failed assumption, how it was found, and what changed. The record should also name the affected versions and say whether earlier scores remain comparable.

Contamination vs saturation

The SWE-bench Verified audit described above also found contamination: every frontier model tested could reproduce the reference patch or verbatim problem details for some tasks. SWE-bench's public repositories and wide use exposed tasks to training. The openness that enabled scrutiny of bad tests also made items easier to encounter before evaluation.

However, if contamination is carefully controlled for during training, hiding the test set by itself does not prevent saturation. A study of 60 language model benchmarks found similar saturation in public and private ones, and concluded that hiding test data does not prevent saturation once a benchmark is widely adopted, meaning a good benchmark falls out of use due to saturation without developers being able to learn from and build on it. What did correspond to lower saturation was expert curation and a larger test set.

This leaves a practical release question: what can we expose for review while protecting active test items?

4. Open sourcing an evaluation strategically

Balancing contamination risks against saturation requires a strategic approach to what content is made public. Rather than treating openness as an all-or-nothing decision, benchmark creators can decide what to release part by part, protecting active test tasks from data leakage while still sharing the underlying infrastructure, grading methods, and reference examples that allow external researchers to audit and build upon the evaluation.

Existing benchmarks show a range of openness. ARC-AGI-2 publishes a training set and a 120-task evaluation set, and holds back semi-private and private sets of 120 tasks each. AILuminate keeps its official prompts confidential, publishes its methods and taxonomy, and keeps the underlying evidence for controlled review by authorized auditors and trusted researchers. Terminal-Bench publishes its tasks and marks their files with a canary string asking that they stay out of training corpora. No public reviewer can check a protected item, so whatever stays closed needs a review route of its own.

Table 1 outlines the core considerations of open sourcing an evaluation: what can be open, where it lives on the Hugging Face Hub, and what may stay protected. It has one row for each component in Figure 2, so you can go straight to the part you are about to release.

PartWhat can be openHow to share on the Hugging Face HubWhat can stay protected with alternatives for public review
TaskSpecifications, categories, construction methods, and a public development splitA dataset repository, with a dataset card recording the source task, changes, license, and limitations Active test items and answers, kept in a separate gated dataset with manual approval of each access request. Release retired items where permissible.
EnvironmentContainer definition, build files, pinned dependencies, and synthetic fixturesIn the dataset repository, declared as an environment type in the dataset card Private data, credentials, licensed assets, or dangerous details. Document how public substitutes differ.
Agent harness and toolsAgent-loop code, tool interfaces, adapters, permissions, and budgetsA link to the harness source and its pinned version, kept in the run record with the configuration used. Give the pinned harness version in the notes field of each 
.eval_results
entry, so it’s next to the score		 Secrets, private services, and sensitive tool implementations. Provide safe substitutes and authorized inspection.
Rollout and tracePublic-task traces, reviewed excerpts, and analysis codeA dataset or storage bucket. Harbor's trace exporter pushes rollout records, and the Hub's trace viewer opens supported session formats. Link scores to these traces through the source field of each 
.eval_results
entry		 Traces exposing tasks, private data, or restricted model behavior. Offer protected analysis and case inspection.
Reference solutionSolution method and code for public examplesThe dataset repository, with each taskSolutions that reveal protected items. Let authorized reviewers check them against the task.
Evaluation harnessRollout orchestration, model configuration, logging, score aggregation, and version recordsA run record kept with the dataset: the job script, model and harness configuration, and package versions. Inspect writes its logs straight to an 
hf://buckets/
path		 Credentials and item-identifying configuration. Keep a reviewable record of the exact restricted run.
VerifierRubrics, grader code, tolerances, and worked examplesThe dataset repository, with each taskReference answers and logic that reveal protected items. Authorized experts should inspect disputed judgments.
Claims and task designIntended use, selection rationale, contextual assumptions, and validation evidenceThe dataset card. Bundle the task dataset, trace dataset, any harness Space, and the paper into one Hub CollectionSensitive source material may need redaction.
ResultsScores, uncertainty, costs, exclusions, and limitations, with the model setup and other reproducibility detailsRegister the dataset as a Hub Benchmark with an 
eval.yaml
. Scores go in each model repo's 
.eval_results/
folder, opened as a pull request, with source linking to the trace dataset. Optionally, also convert them to the EEE schema		 Task-revealing detail in results. Publish safe summaries and arrange review of the underlying evidence.
CorrectionsA correction history that names the affected versionsPull requests and discussions on the repository, with a change log in the card The protected example behind a correction. Still record which versions it affected.

Table 1. What to open, how to share it on the Hugging Face Hub, and what can stay protected, for each evaluation component.

Our own example follows this approach. We released raman-lab as a dataset on the Hub. It includes eight synthetic graphene spectra in Harbor task format, each with its environment, reference fit, verifier, and tolerances. The raw rollouts behind our results are shared as a separate dataset including Harbor trial folders with trajectories and verifier output for all six models. The spectrum generator, analysis code, and results are in a companion GitHub repository, so both the agent harness and the evaluation harness can be inspected and rerun.

In a more sensitive domain, a clinical evaluation could open its environment definition, harness, tool interfaces, and grading framework, with synthetic cases for development use. Patient records and reference answers would stay under controlled access while authorized reviewers inspect disputed judgments. Each restriction should come with a condition for revisiting it.

Strategic open sourcing checklist

We recommend a short checklist, drawn in part from the more comprehensive Agentic Benchmark Checklist. Before releasing or retiring an evaluation, check that another builder can:

  • Identify what it measures, its intended use, and the conditions it leaves out.
  • Find the reusable artifacts, their licenses and versions, and a way to report problems.
  • See how a do-nothing agent scores and, where possible, how a human expert does.
  • Read each score with its uncertainty, and with guidance on what known flaws mean for it.
  • Learn which flaws were found, how they were handled, and how far they could move the results.
  • Know how and when tasks will be refreshed to limit contamination and overfitting.

These release decisions also determine what remains useful when the benchmark no longer separates the systems it was built to compare.

5. Conclusion: giving the evaluation a useful afterlife

Benchmarks have a lifecycle. They are built, adopted, optimized against, and in time stop separating the systems they were made to compare. The saturation study from section 3 rated 29 of its 60 language model benchmarks as highly saturated, with rates rising with age. Saturation is not a failure in itself, since it can mean the capability has arrived.

What a benchmark leaves behind depends on how open it was. Publishing only scores leaves future builders little they can run or adapt. When the tasks, environments, verifiers, and traces are open, each keeps working after the leaderboard stops. A solved task becomes a regression check for a new harness. Its environment and verifier can seed a harder successor. Open benchmarks also get repaired and reissued: MMLU's questions became MMLU-Redux, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 became 2.1 through community contributions. Our own walkthrough is an afterlife of this kind: raman-lab began as one task in a benchmark built for general terminal work.

That is the promise of building evaluations openly. The work that goes into an evaluation can outlive the benchmark itself, giving others a foundation to ask new questions, test new capabilities, and improve on what came before. The more we share what we build and learn, the less each new evaluation has to start from scratch.

If you’re curious what this looks like in practice, then follow our practical example.

Appendix A. Practical example: agentic deployment in a physics lab

Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. Raman spectroscopy shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the frequency of the scattered light; the resulting peaks reveal properties of the material. For graphene, an atom-thick sheet of carbon, the G and 2D peaks near 1580 and 2700 cm⁻¹ identify the number of layers. A third peak, D, appears when the lattice is disordered, and its intensity relative to G can indicate defects. Figure 5 shows the setup.

Figure 5. Our intended setup. A laser lights a graphene sample, and a spectrometer records how the scattered light has shifted. The agent receives that spectrum as a file, fits a curve to each peak, and saves the fitted values. The verifier checks the saved values against reference fits. The curve shown is a sketch, not measured data.

We start by building on a task from an open benchmark. Terminal-Bench 2 already includes raman-fitting: fit a Lorentzian curve, a mathematical peak shape, to each of those two peaks and save eight parameters to 

/app/results.json
. That gives us a runnable starting point for a narrower lab evaluation. We run these on the open source evaluation harness, Harbor. Table 2 lists what the task provides and what to check before reusing each part.
PartIn raman-fittingCheck before reuse
Task
instruction.md
asks for two peak fits saved to 
/app/results.json
.		 Are units, parameter definitions, and the output format explicit?
EnvironmentA pinned container image holding the spectrum; 
task.toml
sets resources and limits.		 Which packages must the agent install? Are resources and permissions suitable?
Agent harness and toolsTerminus-2 connects the model to shell commands.Can the agent inspect what its commands produced?
Rollout and traceOne attempt, recorded in 
agent/trajectory.json
.		 Does the record show what happened before the agent stopped?
Reference solution
solution/solve.sh
runs the known fit.		 Does it pass in the supplied environment?
Evaluation harnessHarbor runs rollouts and collects scores and traces.Are versions and execution settings recorded?
Verifier
tests/test.sh
checks eight fitted values against reference tolerances.		 Does it grade the saved file and accept valid alternative fits?

Table 2. What to check before reusing each component.

Step 1. Define the claim

A good place to start is a claim: a plain statement of what the agent can do, which the evaluation is meant to support. "The agent can fit a Raman spectrum" is a claim, and so is "the agent can process a lab report." From there, you can break the claim into smaller skills that can be checked one at a time, such as reading the file, locating the peaks, and writing the output.

For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio, and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Domain experts can help here. We suggest asking them to choose realistic noise levels, tolerances, and available software, then score examples independently and investigate disagreements. From there, you can break the claim into parts you can check and map each part to what each task tests.

Step 2. Find a starting task

For your own domain, the Hugging Face Hub is a good place to look, under its Benchmark and Environment dataset types. When you find a candidate, it is worth inspecting its instructions, environment, reference solution, and tests. Even a task that models already solve can provide useful infrastructure. From raman-fitting we inherit a working task format. It has only one spectrum, though, and a lab's measurements vary, so we expand on this task further as described in Step 4.

Step 3. Run the task unchanged

Before running any model, it helps to run the reference solution (also called oracle). If it fails, the fault lies in the task, environment, or verifier, and needs to be fixed before you read anything into model failures. After that, you can run the model several times without changing the setup.

We ran Harbor inside an HF Job, which supplied compute for the runner. Each rollout used its own HF Sandbox for commands and files, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. With Harbor's 

hf-sandbox
extra installed and 
HF_TOKEN
set, these commands test the oracle, then run three rollouts with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI.
harbor run -t terminal-bench/raman-fitting \
  -a oracle -e hf-sandbox

OPENAI_API_KEY="$HF_TOKEN" harbor run \
  -t terminal-bench/raman-fitting -k 3 -e hf-sandbox \
  -a terminus-2 -m openai/openai/gpt-oss-120b \
  --ak api_base=https://router.huggingface.co/v1

In these commands, 

-t
names the task, 
-a
the agent, 
-e
the environment, 
-m
the model, and 
-k
the number of rollouts per task.

The model passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

Step 4. Adapt the task

We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

The D-to-G intensity ratio can indicate defects, but its interpretation depends on the laser excitation energy and the disorder regime. An evaluation asking for a "defect ratio" must say which peaks, whether intensity means height or integrated area, and how the result is checked.

The original instruction.md shows why such definitions matter: it asks for x0, gamma, amplitude, and offset without defining them or their units. The reference solution treats them as peak center, half-width at half-maximum, height above background, and background level, and converts the x-axis from nanometres to Raman shift. We put choices like these into the adapted instructions, so that the verifier's requirements are visible. Figure 6 shows the two files side by side.

Figure 6. The 

instruction.md
files for raman-fitting and raman-lab, side by side. The highlighted additions cover the new parts of the claim: the D peak, the defect ratio, and both in the saved results. The remaining part, handling varied measurements, lives in the data: all eight raman-lab tasks share this instruction, and only the spectrum, with its noise and defect level, changes.

The verifier is guided by three rules:

  • Grade what the agent produced: inspect the saved output, not its claim to have finished. τ-bench does this by comparing the final database state with an annotated goal state.
  • State every checked fact in the instruction, including units, parameter conventions, tolerances, and required fields.
  • Generate synthetic data from known parameters so the reference answer is available, then review whether the examples represent the intended problem.

The shared format can stay as it is while the data and checks change. This command creates a task scaffold:

harbor task init my-org/task-01 -p datasets/my-evals

Step 5. Check the evaluation

Before executing more model runs, test the evaluation itself. Here 

datasets/my-evals
contains the adapted tasks.
harbor run -p datasets/my-evals -a oracle -e hf-sandbox
harbor run -p datasets/my-evals -a nop -e hf-sandbox
  • The oracle should pass every task, i.e., the known solution must work in the supplied environment.
  • The no-op agent does nothing, so it should fail every task. A blank exam paper should not pass. A review of agentic benchmarks found one that counted empty responses as successes.
  • A shortcut that skips required work should fail. One way to test this is with a deliberately lazy solution, such as one that outputs a plausible answer without doing the work, to see whether the verifier accepts it. Also try plausible wrong answers and alternative correct methods, to catch both false passes and false failures.

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself. Section 3 explains what that means for verifier design.

Step 6. Run it and read the traces

It is helpful to read both successful and failed rollouts. Harbor records messages, tool calls, and observations in 

agent/trajectory.json
using ATIF, a shared trace format. Grouping failures by cause makes the patterns easier to see: parsing the data, executing a tool, stopping too early, or grading the output.

The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called 

mark_task_complete
in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file.

Figure 7. On 19 of 24 attempts, the agent called 

mark_task_complete
in its first response. Eleven produced no results file, seven passed, and one failed the fit check. Of the five remaining attempts, four passed and one failed the fit check.

Several missing-file failures began with missing NumPy or SciPy. The published task expects the agent to install them; its reference solution starts with a pip install. A lab evaluation of fitting with supplied tools could install and pin them in advance. Dependencies also drift: Terminal-Bench 2.1 repaired nine tasks whose external dependencies had changed after release.

Preinstalling changes the evaluation condition, so keep the model, harness, tasks, and rollout count fixed when comparing the two setups.

Finally, we adapt the setup, repeat the checks in step 5, and rerun. Harbor's trace exporter can prepare records for sharing on the Hub. It is worth reviewing them for protected content first, and keeping both successes and failures so others can investigate the result.

Step 7. Report the score

The right metric depends on the decision you need to make:

  • pass@k asks whether at least one of k rollouts succeeds. Our pass@3 was 7/8: seven tasks succeeded at least once.
  • pass^k asks whether all k rollouts succeed. Our pass^3 was 1/8: one task succeeded every time.

Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more.
